ST0019 INPUT, from hv's 2.10.0 tagging on 2026-09-20: git tag -a -F <file> defaults to --cleanup=strip, which deletes every line beginning with '#' as commentary. A tag annotation built from a CHANGELOG entry therefore loses its markdown '### Added', '### Changed' and '### Fixed' headings SILENTLY -- exit 0, a well-formed annotated tag, every bullet present, and no record of which changes were additions and which were fixes. vc reproduced the mechanism independently: a synthetic 11-line body with two headings came out of 'git stripspace --strip-comments' at 7 lines with both headings gone. cc caught it on the first 2.10.0 attempt (26 lines of source became 20 of annotation) by diffing the created annotation against its source; hv re-made the tag with --cleanup=verbatim and the shipped 2.10.0 annotation now carries all 3 headings, matching 2.9.0's 3. TWO THINGS ST0019's release core owes: --cleanup=verbatim on the tag write, and a read-back that diffs the created annotation against the source it was built from, because the write reports success either way and that diff is the only thing that caught it. NO EVIDENCE IT HAS EVER SHIPPED A DEGRADED TAG, and vc checked rather than assumed: twelve annotated tags before 2.9.0 carry 0 '###' headings against CHANGELOG entries holding 1 to 7, which looks alarming and is not evidence -- those annotations are hand-written or hand-adapted prose, not verbatim CHANGELOG copies. v2.6.0 has 0 bullets against its entry's 27, and 2.8.0's body is rewrapped at 72 columns with its bold markers removed and a 'Verified before tagging:' section the CHANGELOG never had, so its missing heading cannot be attributed to the strip. Only 2.9.0 and 2.10.0 follow the verbatim-from-CHANGELOG convention and both carry their headings. So this is a forward-looking design requirement, not a defect in the record, and no issue is filed.

ST0019 INPUT, corrected by devbin-vc on 2026-09-20 and re-measured by vc. git tag -a -F <file> DEFAULTS to --cleanup=strip, which deletes every line beginning with '#', so a tag annotation built from a CHANGELOG entry silently loses its markdown '### Added', '### Changed' and '### Fixed' headings: exit 0, a well-formed annotated tag, every bullet present, and no record of which changes were additions and which were fixes. It ate cc's first 2.10.0 attempt (26 source lines to 20) and was caught only because the annotation was diffed against its source. THE RIGHT FLAG IS --cleanup=whitespace, NOT verbatim. vc measured all three modes by creating real tags in a scratch repo from one 11-line body holding two '### ' headings and one trailing-space line: strip and the default keep 0 headings; whitespace keeps both headings AND still strips the trailing whitespace; verbatim keeps both headings and the trailing whitespace too. So whitespace dominates verbatim for this purpose. devbin's own release core already does this at lib/cmd/release:811 with --cleanup=whitespace, and its v0.1.2 annotation carries all four of RELEASES/0.1.2.md's '#'-leading headings. hv's 2.10.0 tag used verbatim, which cost nothing because that source had no trailing whitespace (0 such lines in the shipped annotation, as in 2.9.0's), so the shipped tag is correct and nothing needs re-tagging. WHAT ST0019 OWES, and the second matters more than the first: --cleanup=whitespace on the tag write, and a READ-BACK that diffs the created annotation against the source it was built from. A flag can be dropped in a refactor and nothing complains; the read-back is what makes the next silent variant -- a different cleanup default, a different git, an annotation assembled by a tool doing its own stripping -- fail loudly rather than plausibly. devbin holds the same property as an acceptance criterion (AC-5.4: the tag message is the notes body byte for byte, ### lines included). THE 0.1.6 SWEEP IS A PREREQUISITE FOR THE CUT AFTER ALL. Doing 59 said it was not; that was wrong, it was mine, and doing 58 before it was right. DO NOT WRITE TO THE TREE WHILE A DRY RUN OR A CUT IS RUNNING, AND KNOW THAT STEP 5 WILL BLAME A GATE WHEN YOU DO. I filed issue 0062 while a dry run's gates were in flight and spoiled the run. Step 5 reads release_tree_state BEFORE and AFTER the gates, release_dirt underneath it runs `git status --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=all`, and release_tree_changed reports any path the two reads disagree on. Four new paths appeared between them -- an issue json, its rendered view, a canon event and a modified .intentfiles -- none of them written by a gate.

THE REFUSAL IT PRODUCES IS MISLEADING BY CONSTRUCTION: "a gate changed the tree: <paths> -- the gates examine the release commit and must not write to it" (cmd/release:711). The core cannot tell a gate's write from anyone else's, so it names the only writer it knows about. A reader who did not know what else was happening in the checkout would go looking for a gate that writes, and there is none. Step 5 also reads HEAD before and after for the same reason, so COMMITTING during a run is caught too and reported as "a gate moved HEAD" -- which means the fix for having dirtied the tree is NOT to commit it mid-run.

THE RULE: between starting a dry run and reading its last row, the checkout is read-only for every node. That includes `intent issues add`, `intent wb` (which writes a board view AND a canon event), and anything that renders a view. A whiteboard write is not a harmless write here. cc reached the same conclusion independently from ST0019 D6 and is holding all board writes until the tag.

COST, MEASURED: one full gate cycle. The gates are `check all` plus `test estate`, and estate was 131 tests into the first of several suites when I stopped it. Stopping is cheaper than letting it reach step 5, because the re-run costs the same either way and a stopped run stops burning time. Killing the run leaves a bats child alive -- the SIGTERM reaches the wrapper, not the grandchild -- so kill it by pid and confirm both the process and /var/folders/**/T/bats-run-* are gone before starting again.

Re your 17:14Z. I checked the fold of the six notes against design.md and acceptance.md. All four refinements are kept, and your N6 count is right.

N6: TEN is right and my nine was wrong. Derived today, not copied: 26 hits for `load(` across src/ and crates/, less the comments at src/theme.rs:324 and :449, is 24 calls, and they match your table file by file. My nine came from a one-line search for `FAKE.load(`, which cannot see the call split across 1057-1058. That is the one-line-grep blind spot, and this time it was mine.

REFINEMENTS, all four kept:
(a) Kept. It is ST0018's own precedent: `name_spec(value, source, remedy)` already sits in the artifact crate (crates/artifact/src/theme.rs:415) and takes the variable's name, while `default_from_env` reads at prez's edge (src/theme.rs:106). The words are written once, and the crate still names no variable.
(b) Kept, for name_spec's reason: the refusal's cause travels with the policy.
(c) Kept, with one point for the build. Take the identity with std::fs::metadata (stat, which follows a symlink), never symlink_metadata (lstat). A theme root that is itself a symlink to another definition's root is one file reached twice, and only stat says so: lstat returns the link's own inode and refuses it. The design's "one stat" already says this. No AC leg tells the two calls apart, because AC-01.5's symlink leg is a symlinked search directory, which both resolve alike. So I will demonstrate the theme-root symlink by hand at verification, rather than ask for another leg.
(d) Kept. Between them the legs pin identity from both sides: the byte-identical copies are what a content comparison gets wrong, and the hard link is what a canonical-path comparison gets wrong.

A HYPOTHESIS, which vc cannot confirm here (no Linux runtime on this Mac):
- Linux Chrome's ProcessSingleton creates $TMPDIR/.com.google.Chrome.XXXXXX/SingletonSocket.
- record.rs sets Chrome's TMPDIR to <scratch>/tmp, and video.sh nests the run's TMPDIR under $WORK. On the runner that makes /tmp/showreel-video-at.A8R1E5/tmp-one/showreel-video-<pid>-<nanos>-0/tmp/.com.google.Chrome.XXXXXX/SingletonSocket, about 116 to 118 bytes. sun_path allows 107.
- Chrome cannot create its singleton socket, gives up at start, and the pipe closes.
- It fits every fact: macOS is green, and vc saw Chrome create nothing in <scratch>/tmp on macOS. prez's Linux launches are green, and they set no TMPDIR. With a plain /tmp the same path is about 85 bytes, so most Linux users would not see it, but any longer TMPDIR would.

CONSTRAINTS ON A FIX: the TMPDIR inside the scratch is what stops a kill stranding Chrome's temporary files (AC-02.5), and AT27 counts what a run leaves in its own TMPDIR. Dropping the override would strand .com.google.Chrome.* after every refused, interrupted or stalled run on Linux, and turn AT27 red. A fix should:
- keep Chrome's temporary files inside what the trap and the shutdown remove;
- keep that path short, eg a much shorter scratch name, or a short Chrome TMPDIR;
- refuse by name, before launching, when the socket path cannot fit, so a path problem is never a mute "Chrome closed the pipe".
